newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: TENNIS-ENQVIST LEADER OF SWEDEN'S NEW GUARD.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-ENQVIST LEADER OF SWEDEN'S NEW GUARD.

text.p: There was no ceremony to mark the occasion but, in leading the way to the Davis Cup final, Thomas Enqvist has replaced Stefan Edberg, last of the old generation, as Sweden's key tennis player.

Enqvist's hard-fought five-set victory over Czech Daniel Vacek not only clinched Sweden's second Davis Cup final berth in three years, it marked a changing of the guard in his country's illustrious tennis history.
Edberg, winner of six grand slam titles and a member of three victorious Davis Cup teams, is near the end of the last year of his distinguished career.
Enqvist, a 22-year-old right-hander from Stockholm, now shoulders the responsibility carried in the past by the likes of Bjorn Borg, Mats Wilander and Edberg.

"I think we are seeing a big part of the future of Swedish tennis unfolding in front of us," assistant coach Anders Jarryd, who teamed up with Edberg 12 years ago to beat the U.S. in the Davis Cup final, said in an interview.

"Edberg is the last of the old Swedish guard, Enqvist will be the cornerstone of the new guard. This tournament should give him the confidence boost he will need when facing big opponents on big occasions in the future."
Edberg said: "I think even without me they have a great team and can win in the future. And for Enqvist the win against Vacek was important because it should help his confidence in the future."

Enqvist was a pillar in Sweden's victory over the Czechs, dominating Petr Korda in the opening singles match of the tie and then, down 2-1 in sets with a raucous partisan crowd cheering on hometown favourite Vacek, showing the poise of a veteran to regroup and claw his way back into the match.

Instead of wilting under the pressure, Enqvist drew strength from it. He regained the rhythm he had lost earlier in the match, scorching the Prague Sports Hall's Supreme surface with some of the most powerful groundstrokes it will ever see.

"I have never faced a ball coming back at me like that. His shots were unbelievably strong. If he can play like that on the tour he can definitely be in the top five," said a shell-shocked Korda after falling to the world number 14 in straight sets.
But can he reach number one -- his highest ranking was number six in February -- the way his boyhood idols Borg, Wilander and Edberg did?
Swedish non-playing captain Calle Hageskog believes so, but only with hard work and time.
"I think he has the skills to make it. If he continues to work and progress, I really believe he has the tools to be one of (the best), if not the best in the world," he said.
If Enqvist himself believes such words, it doesn't show.

With only eight tournament victories under his belt, he readily acknowledges Edberg's accomplishments -- 41 singles titles and 17 doubles titles and praises one of the tour's greatest without hesitation.
Unassuming and shy, he seems to prefer letting the experienced Edberg handle the crowds of reporters in pre-match and post-match interviews, remaining himself in the background.
"Stefan is no doubt the leader of this team, he's shown over a long period of time that he can play with the best, and off the court he handles himself like a champion as well," Enqvist said.
And does he consider himself an Edberg-in-waiting?
"I hope I can be as successful, or even more so. But there is only one Stefan and I hope to be the only Thomas, that is all I can hope for."
